10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.04.036.abstract: Flexible wire harnesses serve as the "neural network" and "lifeline" of complex electromechanical systems such as aircraft, ships, and automobiles. Its design flaws directly affect manufacturing feasibility and operational safety, and may even lead to catastrophic failures. Owing to their hybrid rigid-flexible constraints, multidimensional deformations, intricate routing, cross-scale, and high-density integration, flexible harnesses exhibit extremely complex characteristics. These characteristics make the design of a digital mock-up for wire harnesses exceptionally challenging. Achieving effective modeling, simulation, analysis, and optimization of wire harnesses during the design phase—thereby enabling early verification of manufacturing compliance and identification of potential service risks—remains a critical challenge in forward design. This challenge has continuously driven the development of theoretical research mode and methodological framework in the field. However, compared with the well-established theories and mature methodologies of forward design of mechanical system, research on forward design of wire harnesses still has obvious shortcomings. It is therefore urgent to systematically sort out technologies and summarize the development trajectory to accelerate progress in this domain. Therefore, this paper surveys the evolution of forward design methodologies of flexible wire harnesses, with a particular focus on assembly configuration, from an intelligent design perspective. It clarifies research directions, development trends, and research opportunities for intelligent approaches in this field. First, this paper summarizes the forward design paradigm for wire harness characteristics, including multi-scale characteristics, the task framework, and the evolution—from manual, digitalization, artificial intelligence to augmented intelligence. It then reviews the current research status of intelligent forward design research for wire harnesses, emphasizing the application of artificial intelligence techniques such as computer vision, traditional machine learning, deep learning, and metaheuristic algorithms. Afterwards, according to the development requirements of new-generation intelligent manufacturing mode, the study further identifies human-machine collaborative augmented intelligence design—integrating emerging technologies such as mixed reality, generative artificial intelligence, and digital twin—as a key future direction. A prospective research framework for augmented intelligence in forward design of wire harnesses is proposed. On this basis, the paper analyzes key challenges and identifies critical research opportunities in four directions. The developmental trends, future framework, and research opportunities presented herein aim to provide systematic reference and forward-looking guidance for future studies on flexible wire harness, contributing to the ongoing advancement of forward design theory.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.04.036.title: From artificial intelligence to augmented intelligence: A review of intelligent forward design of wire harnesses
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.04.036.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.04.028.abstract: This paper introduces LLM-Embodied Agents (LEAs) for manufacturing task allocation by embedding large language model (LLM) driven cognitive capabilities directly into physical production resources. Despite existing efforts in LLM-based multi-agent coordination, current frameworks do not systematically address the heterogeneous constraints prevalent in manufacturing, particularly task-level spatial constraints. Furthermore, existing frameworks treat automated guided vehicles (AGVs) as passive executors rather than autonomous decision-making agents, leaving their coordination potential unexplored. To address heterogeneous manufacturing constraints, we develop coordination strategies among the LEAs that enable systematic reasoning over capability matching, process precedence relationships, and spatial accessibility requirements. We implement Robot LEAs (RLEAs) and Vehicle LEAs (VLEAs), where robots denote industrial robots and vehicles denote AGVs. We systematically compare two decentralized coordination strategies: Robot-Lead Coordination (RLC), where RLEAs select tasks to process, and Vehicle-Lead Coordination (VLC), where VLEAs recruit machines for task execution. We evaluate the strategies across three manufacturing scenarios with different constraints, including sorting (capability constraints), machining (precedence constraints), and disassembly (spatial and precedence constraints). In disassembly tasks, VLC attains 100% constraint satisfaction versus 63% for RLC using GPT-4o, while reducing total token consumption by 41% and API calls by 68%. Cross-model evaluation with Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and DeepSeek-R1 confirms VLC’s robustness across different LLM backbones, while ablation studies demonstrate that failure memory significantly improves RLC performance but provides marginal gains for VLC. Scalability analysis shows VLC scales at a substantially lower rate than RLC as problem size increases.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.04.028.title: Coordination of LLM-Embodied Agents for manufacturing task allocation under constraints
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.04.028.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.008.abstract: Human-robot collaborative assembly (HRCA), which combines human cognitive flexibility with robotic precision, has become a core paradigm for smart manufacturing in Industry 5.0. Dynamic action intention recognition is a key technology for seamless human-robot interaction. However, the complexity of industrial assembly scenarios makes it difficult for collaborative robots to accurately understand the operator's assembly action intentions. Most existing methods rely on graph convolutional networks with fixed skeletal topologies, lacking the capability to capture cross-joint dependencies tailored to different action samples. These approaches depend on a single type of human skeletal feature (e.g., joint coordinates) and fail to effectively integrate multi-level dynamic information (e.g., joint trajectory kinematics and bone-level geometric transformations), resulting in an incomplete semantic representation of human action intention. To address these issues, this paper proposes an HRCA action intention recognition method based on a Dual-stream Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (DS-AGCN) model. Firstly, a simplified human skeletal structure is designed by removing redundant joints irrelevant to assembly actions, making it more suitable for recognizing upper-body movements in HRCA scenarios. Secondly, to enhance the model's generalization capability against operators’ individual differences, six data augmentation strategies are introduced. Then, an adaptive adjacency matrix is incorporated into the proposed method to strengthen the learning of dynamic dependencies between human joints that are not naturally connected. Finally, a dual-stream feature fusion mechanism is proposed. By embedding a motion stream within the joint stream, the operator's assembly actions are characterized from two dimensions: raw joint coordinates and joint motion features, thereby improving the accuracy of HRCA intention recognition. In the experiment, a HRCA experimental platform for a cylinder gear reducer is designed and developed, and an HRCA action video dataset is constructed based on it. The proposed method is experimentally validated using this dataset. The experimental results, including the model's training convergence performance, the enhancement effect of data augmentation strategies and adaptive adjacency matrix, and visualizations of the learning process across different network layers, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Compared with eight other state-of-the-art methods, the proposed method achieves the best performance on four evaluation metrics, with an Accuracy of 96.97%, Precision of 97.08%, Recall of 96.97%, and F1-score of 96.95%, demonstrating its superiority in the recognition accuracy for HRCA intention.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.008.title: Dual-stream adaptive graph convolutional network with enhanced skeleton representation for human-robot collaborative assembly intention recognition
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.008.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.009.abstract: This paper describes an active learning approach for part-to-part iterative machining process optimization using a hybrid surrogate tool life model. A probabilistic interpolating tool life model is developed by combining the empirical Taylor-type tool life equation and the model fit error. The probabilistic tool life model is then used to calculate the machining cost per part distribution. The optimal machining parameters are selected using an expected improvement in machining cost per part criterion. The method is validated numerically using experimental results; the results show a median convergence error of 2.2% after three tests over 400 simulations. The method is validated experimentally on two industrial applications for Ti-6Al-4V roughing resulting in a cost per part reduction greater than 23% after two tests. The described method is a robust solution for rapid convergence to optimal machining parameters in an industrial production environment.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.009.title: Active learning using hybrid surrogate tool life modeling for machining process optimization
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.009.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.012.abstract: Smart manufacturing systems increasingly rely on integrated production, inspection, and maintenance decisions to achieve high economic performance while satisfying stringent quality and reliability constraints under nonstationary operating conditions. Fixed inspection thresholds and periodic maintenance schedules often fail to adapt to evolving equipment states, leading to infeasible operation and suboptimal profit. This paper proposes a new Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)-based Multi-Agent System (MAS) decision-making algorithm for quality-critical smart manufacturing systems, addressing production, inspection, and maintenance decisions within a unified framework. A data-driven wear proxy triggers condition-based maintenance, while XAI fidelity signals dynamically adjust both inspection thresholds and effective maintenance wear thresholds when explanation fidelity indicates unreliable predictions. Global feasibility with respect to false-positive and false-negative constraints is enforced through an augmented Lagrangian optimization that supports policy parameters over long horizons. Case studies using large-scale industrial data demonstrate that the proposed MAS-XAI policy significantly outperforms both periodic maintenance strategies and a Deep Q-Network (DQN) policy. Relative to DQN, MAS-XAI achieves a 14.28% profit increase. Compared with periodic maintenance, it reduces maintenance interventions by 55.2% while maintaining a strict false-negative rate of 0.82%. The results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm improves operational robustness and economic performance in smart manufacturing systems under dynamic conditions.
keywords: Integrated Production and Maintenance Decision Making
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.012.title: A new explainable artificial intelligence algorithm integrated with multi-agent system for joint decision-making of smart manufacturing systems
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.012.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.010.abstract: Reconfigurable manufacturing systems (RMSs) utilize reconfigurable machine tools and flexible material handling systems to enhance adaptability and responsiveness, supporting growing demand for mass customization. Nevertheless, tight coupling among production, transportation, and reconfiguration decisions in dynamic environments makes system-level coordinated decision-making highly challenging. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches, constrained by inadequate state representations, fail to capture the heterogeneous and tightly coupled interactions inherent in RMS operations. To address this challenge, we propose an edge-enhanced heterogeneous graph reinforcement learning approach (EHGRL) for the dynamic coordination of integrated production and transportation in RMSs. The problem is formulated as a Markov decision process, where system states are represented by an integrated reconfiguration-transportation disjunctive graph that explicitly encodes heterogeneous entities and their interactions. An edge-enhanced tri-relational heterogeneous attention network is further developed to embed the graph by incorporating edge-enhanced attention with multi-level node-edge-semantic information fusion, enabling expressive state representations and effective end-to-end decisions. Extensive experiments on 760 instances demonstrate that EHGRL outperforms the compared methods, achieving up to 75.1% and 71.5% average relative percentage deviation reductions relative to the best baseline in comparative and generalization studies, respectively, while maintaining millisecond-level online inference, highlighting its robustness, generalization capability, and deployment potential in complex RMS environments.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.010.title: Dynamic coordinated decision-making for integrated production and transportation in reconfigurable manufacturing systems via edge-enhanced heterogeneous graph reinforcement learning
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.010.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.016.abstract: In the autonomy problem of large-scale, mass-customized 3D printing orders, three steps are usually involved: allocating orders among enterprises, assigning parts to 3D printers, and arranging parts on the printer’s build platform. Among these steps, the layout of parts on a 3D printer serves as the underlying layer of the autonomy loop, providing the basis for obtaining feedback during part-equipment matching and enabling real-time adjustments. It also affects the allocation of orders among enterprises. Currently, artificial intelligence (AI) agents specifically designed for part layout remain underdeveloped, and practical engineering applications still rely heavily on manual operations. Against this backdrop, this paper proposes a novel reinforcement-learning-enhanced autonomous layout method for 3D printing parts using a small-parameter vision-language model (SPVLM), aiming to provide an effective AI agent solution for the autonomous parts layout stage. We propose an autonomy architecture for large-scale, mass-customized 3D printing. For the part layout problem in 3D printing, we propose a visual-text evidence enhancement method and construct a dataset of 10,000 scene samples. We further propose an improved generative reinforcement policy optimization (GRPO) technique to enhance the layout decision-making capability of SPVLMs. Finally, based on the SPVLM, we build an AI agent using a reasoning and acting (ReAct) architecture. The AI agent continually acquires part-layout experience through a memory-augmentation strategy and supports lightweight deployment. A representative subset of the dataset is made publicly available at: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1RTYGFb2dvBAsXXD5v7OTXq07QpIXMcTA?usp=drive_link
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.016.title: A novel reinforcement-learning-enhanced autonomous layout method for 3D printing parts using a small-parameter vision-language model
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.016.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.015.abstract: The performance of aeroengines, as complex and precise thermodynamic systems, is highly influenced by assembly quality. However, the lack of integration between assembly and test-run stages hampers the effective use of massive assembly data for closed-loop optimization. Moreover, in mass production characterized by unit-oriented structural design, there is no scalable method to pre-evaluate unit assembly quality. These limitations lead to greater variability in full-machine performance and higher test-run failure rates, which causes rework and significantly increases manufacturing costs. To address this, a unit-oriented aeroengine assembly and test-run linkage framework is proposed. Firstly, assembly data are used to construct network and dynamics models to characterize unit assembly quality. Combined with resilience theory, the unit assembly quality evaluation index and qualified interval are proposed, enabling pre-evaluation and filtering of units before full-machine assembly. Next, using Bayesian theory, the unit-oriented full-machine test-run performance prediction model is constructed, capturing the causal links and probability mappings between unit combinations and full-machine performance. Finally, integrating the above models, the current assembly and test-run process is optimized by building a qualified unit library, predicting the full-machine test-run pass probability of unit combinations, and using feedback from test results to generate actionable assembly recommendations, thereby achieving coordination between assembly and testing. According to the experimental results, the dynamic model achieves fitting errors as low as 2%, underscoring its high accuracy and reliability in characterizing unit assembly quality, while the test-run results and maintenance records provide strong empirical validation. This framework improves coordination between assembly and test-run processes, reduces failure and rework, and supports unit interchangeability and optimal matching. It also underpins the development of digital engineering and intelligent assembly, with significant engineering value and broad application prospects.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.015.title: Unit-oriented aeroengine assembly and test-run linkage framework: A data-driven complex network approach
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.015.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.017.abstract: To advance automation in the remanufacturing sector, this paper proposes a novel spatial disassembly constraint modelling method that integrates cross-modal deep learning with the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). A significant challenge in robotic disassembly is accurately identifying spatial constraints for used products, which often exhibit uncertain conditions and structural deviations from original designs. To address this, we introduce a cross-modal deep learning technique that unifies the detection mechanism for both captured images of used products and CAD models of original products, effectively resolving multimodal data fusion issues during model training. Furthermore, we leverage LLMs to construct and match semantic graphs based on the spatial positional relationships among components. This allows for the precise identification of the optimal matching CAD model and the correct numbering of detected components, thereby deriving specific spatial constraints for each component. The rigour and performance of this method are validated through a case study involving the removal of used bolster springs from railway wagon bogies on a robotic platform. The results demonstrate that the proposed method enables robots to accurately construct spatial disassembly constraints under complex and uncertain conditions, facilitating automated disassembly operations.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.017.title: Bridging 2D vision and 3D CAD: Integrating cross-modal deep learning and LLM-assisted semantic graph reasoning for spatial disassembly constraint modelling
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.05.017.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.020.abstract: With the advent of the Industrial 5.0 era, scenarios such as intelligent manufacturing and equipment operation and maintenance (O&M) have increased the requirements for high-quality human–machine interaction. Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in terms of semantic understanding and generation for industrial question answering, fault diagnosis, and intelligent O&M, they face challenges such as hallucination and a high computational cost. To address these issues, CoLMAgent, a collaborative agentic AI system that integrates large and small models for industrial intelligent human–machine interactions, is proposed. First, a semantic structuring model (SSM) is constructed to parse users’ unstructured natural language into a domain-specific structured semantic representation. Second, we propose a process agent model (PAM) paradigm that modularly orchestrates small models according to the process workflows to form executable task-specific processes. Third, a collaborative matching mechanism for large–small models based on multidimensional evaluation is designed to select the agent that best meets the process–agent user requirements; moreover, prompt templates are used to inject the agents’ computed results into the LLM generation process, thereby improving the professionalism of industrial human–machine interactions. Experimental results on a Chinese intelligent O&M question-answering dataset from real engineering scenarios indicate that CoLMAgent outperforms the baseline models in terms of the BERTScore, RQUGE and BARTScore, thus showing that it achieves high-quality content generation for industrial human–machine interactions.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.020.title: CoLMAgent: A collaborative agentic AI system that integrates large and small models for industrial intelligent human–machine interactions
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.020.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.003.abstract: Industry 4.0 requires transparent and reliable prediction of manufacturing outcomes, which is often constrained by scarce data and incomplete physical mechanisms. These constraints are particularly severe for bent bilayer metal tubes, whose springback prediction is essential for process planning. This work proposes MET-Net, a mechanism-guided neural framework for explainable transfer learning that reuses abundant single-layer springback knowledge for data-scarce bilayer prediction. MET-Net maps bilayer cross-section parameters to an equivalent single-layer representation through a differentiable equivalent-section module, whose adaptation is restricted to two physically meaningful correction parameters. The model is trained in two stages: physics-based initialization and single-layer pretraining, followed by conservative bilayer fine-tuning with sparse physics-residual guardrails, and a lightweight affine calibrator. On a copper-aluminum rotary draw bending case, MET-Net achieves a median RMSE of 0.4835° using only 100 bilayer samples, approaching the accuracy of a single-layer baseline trained on ten times more data. A paired zero-shot environment-perturbation evaluation further indicates stable performance under environment-level perturbations. Beyond accuracy, MET-Net supports manufacturing transparency through a structurally interpretable mechanism pathway, DeepLIFT-based training monitoring, and post-hoc diagnosability analyses. These strategies identify validity regimes of the embedded equivalent-section theory and quantify where systematic correction is required. MET-Net therefore provides accurate bilayer springback prediction together with actionable mechanism insight for process planning under data scarcity and incomplete physics.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.003.title: MET-Net: An equivalent-section mechanism-guided neural framework for explainable transfer learning in bilayer tube springback prediction under data scarcity and incomplete physical mechanisms
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.003.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.009.abstract: The transition toward sustainable manufacturing requires Surface Mount Technology (SMT) lines to adopt energy-carbon aware production scheduling. Traditional paradigms treat machines as discrete states, failing to capture the continuous thermodynamic inertia of thermal equipment like reflow ovens. Coupled with dynamic electricity prices and fluctuating carbon factors, classical optimization and standard multi-agent reinforcement learning become inadequate. To address the deep coupling of discrete manufacturing logic and continuous thermodynamics, we reformulate the scheduling problem as a semi-Markov decision process and propose a novel graph meta-reinforcement learning architecture termed GMeta-MATD3. Specifically, graph neural networks are utilized to extract spatial–temporal topologies across production and microgrid networks. To navigate environmental non-stationarity, a meta-learning module is embedded within each agent to infer latent physical contexts and predict peer behaviors, enabling temporal energy arbitrage via deliberate “wait” actions. Additionally, an attention-based centralized critic dynamically decomposes joint values to resolve the multi-agent credit assignment problem. Extensive experiments on real SMT data coupled with IEEE distribution systems demonstrate significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. GMeta-MATD3 achieves the best Pareto front, yielding a 13.1h makespan, 1020.5 RMB energy cost, 810.2 kgCO2 emissions, a 1.5% tardiness rate, and zero grid violations. Crucially, its thermodynamic stepping mechanism reduces transition energy from 12.5 to 3.2 kWh/batch, and proactive peak avoidance cuts the load peak-to-valley difference by 34.5%, maintaining daily carbon intensity below 0.55 kgCO2/kWh. Scalability tests confirm that executing 500-batch schedules in under 500 ms.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.009.title: Proactive energy-carbon aware production scheduling in SMT lines: A novel graph meta-reinforcement learning approach
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.009.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.001.abstract: In high-precision machining processes such as turbine blade manufacturing, optimizing process parameters is crucial for improving production efficiency and precision. However, process parameter optimization in current industrial practice still suffers from two major drawbacks: the slow convergence speed of high-dimensional parameter optimization and the protection of manufacturing data privacy. To address these issues, this article proposes a Sophia Extended (SophiaX) optimization algorithm under the novel personalized federated learning (DecePFL) framework. Specifically, the SophiaX algorithm is proposed, which efficiently utilizes second-order information through adaptive estimates of diagonal Hessian, significantly accelerating the convergence of high-dimensional process parameter optimization for complex blades. Furthermore, the DecePFL framework is constructed, which achieves personalized federated learning (PFL) through parameter decoupling and performs decentralized federated aggregation, thereby ensuring the privacy protection of industrial data. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we conduct experiments on three series of aviation turbine blades (Blade A, Blade B, and Blade C). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly improves optimization efficiency, reducing optimization iterations from 84 to 27 for Blade A, from 80 to 28 for Blade B, and from 90 to 38 for Blade C.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.001.title: Adaptive parameter optimization for turbine blade manufacturing: A novel personalized federated learning framework
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.001.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.023.abstract: Many human working environments are arduous, and entirely replacing on-site workers with robots remains challenging. To address this issue, this study proposes a teleoperation and manipulation skill learning framework for physical avatar robots. For teleoperation, a real-time, dual-arm motion retargeting method based on a graph isomorphism attention network (GIAN) and robust kalman filtering (RKF) has been developed. This method eliminates the need for manually labeled human-to-robot joint mappings. By representing human motion as graph-structured data and leveraging a learning approach with kinematic physical constraints, accurate retargeting is achieved. The RKF is adopted to suppresses noise and outliers for enhancing stability. For skill learning, the study introduces a graph information-embedded reinforcement learning (GIERL) method that integrates imitation and reinforcement learning. Graph features extracted by GIAN are incorporated into both the observation space and reward design, enabling efficient acquisition of dual-arm manipulation skills. Furthermore, a shared control strategy is designed by integrating GIERL with GIAN to augment manipulation, forming a synergistic closed loop between perception and decision-making. Experiments involving desktop organization, as well as dual-arm box lifting and transportation in both simulated and real environments, demonstrate the superior performance and practicality of the proposed framework.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.023.title: A graph isomorphism attention network and graph information embedded reinforcement learning-based dual-arm robot teleoperation and manipulation skill acquisition method
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.023.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.021.abstract: Human-robot collaborative (HRC) assembly is pivotal to modern manufacturing, yet it suffers from critical bottlenecks that hinder its performance. The fusion of visual, textual, and operational multimodal information remains inefficient, and human-robot task partitioning is often ambiguous. This ambiguity arises from inadequate integration of domain knowledge with perceptual outputs, while manual assembly operations lack consistency and a notable disjunction exists between abstract task reasoning and embodied robotic execution. These issues collectively impede the intelligence and coordination of HRC assembly systems. To resolve these issues, this study proposes an end-to-end Vision-Language Model (VLM)-enhanced embodied intelligent framework for HRC assembly’s cognitive reasoning and autonomous execution. The framework adopts a closed-loop architecture with four cascaded core modules, synergistically supporting perception, knowledge reasoning, human-robot interaction, and autonomous execution. First, a VLM-driven multimodal cognition module innovatively fuses VLMs with BERT (textual semantic processing) and ResNet-50 (visual feature extraction), capturing fine-grained features of assembly personnel, parts and tools to generate structured perceptual representations via semantic triplets and state matrices. Second, a domain knowledge-driven reasoning module is developed, which constructs an assembly knowledge graph by extracting semantic triplets from corpora via VLMs and encodes domain experience into machine-readable form. It adopts Graph RAG for semantic alignment, conflict detection and structured retrieval, and leverages LLM-aided reasoning to decompose global tasks into robotic and manual subtasks with clear boundaries. Third, an AR-assisted assembly guidance module is proposed to enable seamless HRC interaction and precise manual operations through multi-dimensional guidance. It covers visual-textual prompts, 3D positioning overlays, real-time monitoring and remote consultation, translating reasoned manual subtasks into actionable guidelines. Finally, a VLM-driven robotic code generation module realizes autonomous execution by generating modular action functions, sequences and trajectory parameters based on reasoned task representations. Integrated with hardware components, it uses an embodied controller to convert abstract robotic subtasks into concrete physical operations. Comparative experiments with traditional models and LLMs confirm the proposed HRC assembly system’s superiority.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.021.title: Vision language model-enhanced embodied intelligence for AR-assisted HRC assembly: Multimodal cognition, task reasoning, and autonomous execution
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.06.021.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.005.abstract: Predictive maintenance for manufacturing processes has become critically urgent to enhance system reliability in modern manufacturing. This paper proposes a cross-modal large language model for conversational diagnosis of machining process, where an interactive decision-making system that integrates multi-source sensor data fusion and knowledge enhancement was constructed. Firstly, the study introduces a knowledge guided graph fusion method to address challenges in information integration. Secondly, a cross-modal image–text generation model is developed to achieve low-parameter alignment between time-series imaging features and language models, enabling the generation of interpretable diagnostic reports. Finally, to tackle knowledge fragmentation issues of general large language models in industrial scenarios, a domain knowledge graph is constructed, covering tool wear mechanisms and the impact of machining parameters. A parameter-efficient fine-tune strategy is employed to inject structured knowledge, mitigating knowledge hallucination issues inherent in general large models. Experimental results demonstrate that the framework achieves an accuracy of 94.2% in tool remaining useful life prediction tasks, representing a 11% improvement over traditional deep learning models, while providing dynamic maintenance recommendations through natural language interaction. This research offers theoretical support for the development of human–machine collaborative machining systems in intelligent manufacturing, advancing online monitoring technologies toward interpretable and interactive paradigms.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.005.title: Chat with the manufacturing process: A knowledge-guided cross-modal large language model for machining condition predictive maintenance
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.005.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.015.abstract: In manufacturing systems, shop-floor operators frequently adjust algorithmically generated schedules based on their tacit knowledge. However, realizing these modifications through existing interfaces is typically labor-intensive and time-consuming. We identify two fundamental gaps underlying these difficulties: the intent-execution gap and the change-comprehension gap. The intent-execution gap arises from the disparity between high-level user intents expressed in natural language and the sequence of low-level, executable actions required by the existing interfaces. Subsequently, the change-comprehension gap emerges because operators must manually compare the original and modified schedules to recover situational awareness. To address both gaps within a single coherent framework, we propose MARS, a multi-agent rescheduling framework leveraging large language models for human-centric decision support. MARS enables operators to express modification intents directly in natural language, automatically translating them into executable code that updates scheduling parameters or schedules. Designed for computationally constrained manufacturing environments, the framework integrates two agents: a schedule modifier and an explainer. The schedule modifier combines a scheduler re-run classifier and a modification type classifier within a parameter-efficient multi-adapter architecture, and employs a level-wise asymmetric in-context learning (ICL) strategy for the modification code generator. The explainer combines a tree-based causal chain with ICL to describe cascading schedule changes. Experimental results on the unrelated parallel machine scheduling problem demonstrate MARS’s superior ability to accurately execute user requests and generate transparent explanations, alongside robust generalization to larger problems. Ultimately, MARS provides a single natural language interface that effectively supports human decision-making in user-driven rescheduling, bridging both the intent-execution and change-comprehension gaps.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.015.title: MARS: Multi-Agent Rescheduling Framework with Large Language Models for Human-Centric Manufacturing
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.015.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.007.abstract: This research proposes a Causal-Aware Diffusion Language Model (CA-DLM) for interpretable generation of defective images to address the scarcity of defective samples in industrial settings. Firstly, a causal inference mechanism is integrated into DLM to establish a causal mapping among “natural language instructions, model causal variables, and defective image generation”. The counterfactual causal intervention strategy enables interpretable, fine-grained control over defect, texture, and background features during image generation. Secondly, a learnable Structural Causal Model (SCM) is constructed to disentangle semantic features into causal and non-causal variables, effectively separating useful semantic features from confounders during image generation. A causal loss function is also designed to enforce sparsity and acyclicity in the SCM, guiding the model toward a causally consistent structure. Finally, the causal intervention approach is designed to perform do-intervention on SCM to achieve interpretable defective image generation. The do-intervention activates relevant causal variables and suppresses non-causal variables according to the learned SCM, thereby enabling precise control over key defect attributes while preserving the consistency of texture and background. Comparative experiments across three public datasets show that CA-DLM enables interpretable, controllable generation of high-fidelity defective images, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Detection models trained on CA-DLM generated images achieve significant improvements in downstream defect detection tasks, with accuracy exceeding 95%. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, showing that high-fidelity defective images can be generated using only 30% of causal variables.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.007.title: CA-DLM: Causal-aware diffusion language model for interpretable industrial defective image generation
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.007.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.019.abstract: To address the challenges encountered in the automated assembly of aeroengine blades, where non-conformal insertion, irregular boundary features, and insufficient pose alignment accuracy occur between the blade root and disk slot, this paper develops a force-vision-guided robotic assembly platform. Based on the 3D point cloud measured by structured light, a pose estimation method integrating geometric priors (GP) and reinforcement learning (RL) strategies is proposed. Firstly, the key tasks and coordinate transformations in the automated blade assembly process are systematically defined, the geometric constraint mechanisms during assembly are analyzed, and a mathematical chain linking point cloud input to robotic motion control is constructed for pose estimation. Subsequently, during the coarse registration stage, three types of geometric priors—planar constraint, coaxial constraint, and boundary contour constraint—are incorporated to improve the accuracy and robustness of initial pose alignment. In the fine registration stage, the pose refinement of point clouds is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and a hybrid sparse–dense reward mechanism is designed. The Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm is then employed to efficiently optimize the registration policy. Finally, assembly validation experiments were performed on both dovetail and fir-tree blades using the CoppeliaSim simulation platform and a self-developed structured- light measurement system. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior performance over existing registration algorithms in pose estimation accuracy, alignment stability, and assembly feasibility. This study provides an effective and generalizable solution for the intelligent assembly of complex structural components.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.019.title: A pose estimation method for aeroengine blade assembly based on geometric priors and reinforcement learning
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.019.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.014.abstract: Safety is a crucial requirement for robotic systems operating in manufacturing environments, where perception and motion errors lead to unsafe physical interactions and process failures. While recent advancements in embodied AI and learning-based robotic systems have significantly improved adaptability, their black-box nature and sensitivity to uncertainties make safety assurance challenging. In response to such challenges, this article provides a comprehensive review of safety-oriented robotic perception and motion planning, along with complementary safety layers such as Digital Twins (DTs) that support the validation and monitoring of AI-driven robotic systems in manufacturing. In particular, our review first establishes optimization- and feasibility-based problem formulations to analyze and categorize this broad topic from a unified perspective. Then, we discuss mathematical principles and methodologies for improving safety in robotic perception and motion planning, including their learning-based counterparts, as well as their synergies with existing safety layers in smart manufacturing. Finally, we identify key challenges and future research directions toward safer and more trustworthy AI-driven robotic manufacturing.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.014.title: Toward provably safe AI-driven perception and motion planning for robotic manufacturing: A review
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.014.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.016.abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) are increasingly adopted in smart manufacturing to enable real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and decision support. However, deploying high-fidelity digital twins continuously across complex manufacturing systems, characterized by multiple processing stations, heterogeneous machines, and autonomous mobile robots, remains computationally prohibitive. To address this challenge, this paper proposes an Adaptive Fidelity Digital Twin (AFDT) framework that dynamically adjusts simulation fidelity at runtime based on predicted system criticality. The framework integrates three hierarchical fidelity levels: (i) a low-fidelity system-level model for continuous monitoring of aggregate production dynamics, (ii) a medium-fidelity station-level discrete-event model for localized operational diagnosis, and (iii) a high-fidelity machine-level physics-based model for detailed equipment health assessment. An event-triggered fidelity scheduler governs transitions between these levels using manufacturing-relevant indicators such as persistent blockage, starvation, and abnormal resource utilization. The proposed framework is validated through a case study of an automotive parts manufacturing system involving multiple product types and mobile robots. Results demonstrate that the AFDT framework selectively activates high-fidelity models only during disruptive events, achieving substantial reductions in cumulative computational cost compared to static high-fidelity digital twin configurations while preserving diagnostic capability for root-cause analysis. The findings indicate that adaptive fidelity management offers a scalable and computationally efficient approach for operational digital twin deployment in complex manufacturing environments.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.016.title: Adaptive-fidelity digital twin framework for complex smart manufacturing system
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.016.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.022.abstract: Incremental sheet forming (ISF) enables flexible manufacturing of complex components, but localized thinning and ductile fracture still restrict its industrial application. Physical trial-and-error tests and finite element (FE) simulations are also time-consuming for repeated process refinement. To address this issue, this study proposes a Physics-Guided Digital Twin (PG-DT) framework incorporating a Physics-Guided Analytical Fracture Predictor (PG-AFP) for pre-machining fracture-risk evaluation. The analytical model calculates kinematic contact boundaries, extracts local strain increments, evaluates stress-state variables, and accumulates ductile damage using the Modified Mohr-Coulomb (MMC3) criterion, without requiring full-field FE discretization for fracture-risk screening. Experimental validation shows that the relative prediction errors for fracture depth remain below 8.5% under different geometric and kinematic conditions. In the benchmark case, the analytical engine completes global damage mapping in 13.35 s, corresponding to a 997-fold reduction in computation time compared with the explicit FE model. The rapid damage evaluation enables unsafe candidate strategies to be screened and refined before machine deployment. The parametric analysis explains how key process parameters affect the evaluated stress state and damage evolution. Material-specific formability evaluations are conducted for AA6061-T6 and Ti-6Al-4V. Finally, the practical viability of the PG-DT workflow is demonstrated through the fracture-free manufacturing of a twisted radial-groove freeform component and a customized cranial prosthesis.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.022.title: Mechanism-driven Digital Twin for proactive fracture prediction in incremental forming: A physics-guided analytical approach
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.022.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.003.abstract: As core components of aero-engines, the surface precision of blisks directly determines the aerodynamic performance and service reliability of the entire engine. During milling on CNC machine tools, workpiece deformation is primarily driven by mechanical factors and further perturbed by thermal effects, exhibiting strong nonlinearity and multi-factor coupling. Despite extensive research, existing prediction methods encounter significant bottlenecks: (1) multi-source monitoring signals are highly aliased and non-stationary, hindering the precise decoupling of physical features reflecting machining mechanisms; (2) limited sample sizes and sparse parameter distributions in target domains restrict the model's generalization capabilities; (3) the complex nonlinear mapping relationships inherent in machining processes are difficult to learn effectively. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a machining deformation prediction model (ATL-PAMDF) based on adaptive transfer learning integrated with physics-informed guidance and Auto-MultiDeF feature extraction. Firstly, the Auto-MultiDeF module is developed to accurately extract and fuse component features from multi-channel aliased signals via a multi-scale decomposition and multi-channel fusion mechanism. Secondly, a pre-training and fine-tuning transfer paradigm under joint multi-channel reconstruction is constructed to facilitate rapid model convergence under sparse sample conditions. Finally, a mechanical model with error compensation is embedded into the training process as a structural prior, guiding the network to learn deformation responses consistent with physical laws. Multi-point deformation prediction experiments on a self-collected blade dataset demonstrate that the proposed ATL-PAMDF model achieves superior prediction accuracy and stability compared to state-of-the-art methods (RMSE&MAE at least 35% and 24% lower, respectively). The results validate its exceptional performance in complex physical scenarios and under aliased, small-sample machining conditions. The proposed method also offers an extensible solution for deformation prediction of other workpieces in CNC machining.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.003.title: Multi-information guided adaptive transfer learning for multi-point deformation prediction of blades in CNC machining based on Auto-MultiDeF
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.003.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.021.abstract: Throughput bottleneck detection is a well-established research topic. However, comparatively less attention has been paid to what should follow once the bottleneck station has been identified. In particular, limited attention has been given to diagnosing its underlying causes and identifying the internal areas whose improvement could most effectively reduce bottleneck-station cycle time. To address this gap, this paper makes two main contributions. First, it formalizes the notion of sub-bottleneck as the sub-cycle period within the selected bottleneck station with the greatest expected potential to reduce station cycle time and potentially improve the production rate when the station remains the effective throughput constraint. Second, it proposes a dynamic and data-driven framework for sub-bottleneck identification based on the Steptime methodology and a sub-bottleneck scoring algorithm. Under the Steptime methodology, each sub-cycle period is defined as the total activation time of its corresponding step in the sequential process, referred to as the Steptime. The framework is formulated for sequential processes represented according to the GRAFCET methodology standardized in IEC 60848. The framework was evaluated on an industrial production line at Fagor Arrasate S. Coop., located in Arrasate, Spain. A GRAFCET-consistent counterfactual benchmark showed that SBScore selected the candidate with the largest expected cycle-time-reduction potential in all nine product references, achieving the highest agreement among the evaluated ranking criteria. The results revealed performance-degrading patterns in the bottleneck station, including upper-tail spreads of up to 541.8 ms in some Steptimes and bimodal behavior in others.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.021.title: A data-driven framework for sub-bottleneck detection in sequential production systems based on the Steptime methodology
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.07.021.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.016.abstract: Production capacity allocation in multi-tier manufacturing industry chains requires coordinated decisions under heterogeneous node capabilities, private local information, and dynamic demand. Centralized optimization scales poorly in such networks, while flat multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods lack explicit leader–follower coordination and are affected by non-stationary policy updates. This paper proposes chain-leader-guided Stackelberg proximal policy optimization (CSPPO), a hierarchical MARL method built on independent PPO. The problem is formulated as a hierarchical decentralized partially observable Markov decision process. The chain leader broadcasts privacy-preserving global guidance, followers execute decentralized capacity allocation policies, and Stackelberg sequential update mechanism (SSUM) separates follower and leader updates to reduce non-stationarity. Experiments include nine simulated industrial chain instances and an automotive glass case. The method is evaluated against ablation variants and other MARL methods. CSPPO stabilizes rapidly and achieves the highest order fulfillment rate (OFR) among the MARL baselines, with competitive Cost and production capacity load balance (PCLB) trade-offs. In the automotive glass case, it improves OFR by 12.0%, reduces Cost by 4.6%, and reduces average changeover frequency (ACF) by 91.6%. These results show that CSPPO can coordinate production capacity allocation in complex industrial chains.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.016.title: CSPPO: A multi-agent reinforcement learning method for production capacity allocation in manufacturing industry chains
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.016.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.002.abstract: The increasing relevance of circular manufacturing and repair oriented production requires adaptive and data-driven process planning approaches capable of handling highly variable products, uncertain component conditions, and incomplete process information. Conventional automation methods for assembly and disassembly are typically optimized for repetitive high volume manufacturing and are therefore not directly suitable for flexible repair environments. This work proposes a methodology for Digital Twin-based lifecycle management to support adaptive (dis-)assembly planning in circular repair factories. The methodology integrates heterogeneous lifecycle data into a unified Digital Twin environment and utilizes simulation-driven methods to evaluate robotic grasp feasibility, assembly accessibility, end effector suitability, and process constraints prior to physical execution. The novelty of this work lies in integrating lifecycle data, adaptive execution strategies, and simulation-driven planning into a unified framework for flexible circular repair operations. The framework combines robotic grasp planning, simulation-based (dis-)assembly analysis, and decision-making for robot-guided, collaborative, or manual execution. Lifecycle data further enhances efficiency through data-driven optimization methods such as assembly group and geometry-based grasp planning. While prototypical implementations are provided for robotic grasp planning and optimization methods, the overall lifecycle-driven framework and execution decision strategies remain conceptual. Validation results demonstrate grasp feasibility analysis, quantitative comparison of robot and end effector configurations, and geometric approximation through manufacturing data integration. Overall, the implemented modules indicate the potential to increase process success, and reduce replanning effort for flexible circular repair processes.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.002.title: A methodology for Digital Twin-based lifecycle management to support adaptive (dis-)assembly planning in circular repair factories
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.002.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.005.abstract: The inspection and testing of high-safety special equipment (HSSE) is crucial for ensuring its safe and stable operation. However, two core tasks still require substantial manual effort: damage mode analysis requires synthesizing dispersed damage-related knowledge, while equipment quality grading involves determining and applying standard-specified rules. Existing LLM-based research augmented with RAG mainly focuses on information retrieval and Q&A, lacking mechanisms to autonomously and deterministically execute context-dependent rules. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the special equipment inspection and testing agent (SEIT-Agent), an AI Agent framework that integrates an LLM-based planner, a specialized tool library, an experience memory pool and a domain knowledge base. The tool library encapsulates quality grading rules for reliable autonomous grading, while the knowledge base integrates damage mode information and is accessible to the LLM via a hybrid vector–keyword RAG approach. The experience memory pool stores successful task execution trajectories to enhance consistency and accuracy in repetitive quality grading tasks. Furthermore, we introduce an expert-guided risk-aware LLM evaluation strategy where domain experts define critical and supporting assessment points and an external large-scale LLM evaluates response quality under a critical-point gating mechanism. Experiments on real-world data from an HSSE enterprise demonstrate that SEIT-Agent outperforms baseline methods on two core tasks.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.005.title: SEIT-Agent: An experience memory enhanced inspection and testing agent for high-safety special equipment with risk-aware LLM evaluation

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.012.abstract: Predictive maintenance creates industrial value only when uncertain health evidence leads to an appropriate intervention under asymmetric failure costs and operational constraints. We present Rec-PdM, a decision-calibrated recursive multi-agent system for uncertainty-aware prescriptive maintenance. Its six decision agents maintain specialized beliefs about asset condition, fault state, remaining useful life, economic risk, action selection, and verification; production-impact and human-prescription interfaces connect these beliefs to factory context and operator-facing decisions. RecursiveLink reconciles local beliefs with downstream decision consequences while preserving the provenance of each update. The method treats maintenance as a partially observable degradation process and calibrates prediction and uncertainty against decision regret, tail risk, feasibility, and communication overhead. Evaluation on six public datasets spans degradation prognosis, process failure, vibration-based diagnosis, and acoustic anomaly detection, with controlled decision studies of cost asymmetry, coordination, resource constraints, dependent faults, and operating drift. RecursiveLink achieves the best mean-cost rank among the evaluated coordination mechanisms, while calibrated Rec-PdM ranks in the top two in 98.3% of the evaluated cost regimes without an unexpected failure. Under shared fleet constraints, the coordinator remains in the top two by mean cost in 88.8% of 240 scenarios; prequential recursive guarding reduces unserved failures from 70 to 5 under drift. These results show that decision cost, tail risk, and traceable coordination complement predictive accuracy when maintenance evidence must be converted into action.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.012.title: Rec-PdM: Decision-calibrated recursive multi-agent systems for uncertainty-aware prescriptive maintenance in smart manufacturing

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.002.abstract: Accurate recognition of fine-grained work operations in industrial logistics environments remains a challenging open problem due to the complexity of human motion, environmental variability, and the heterogeneous nature of sensor data. In this paper, we present PackFormer, a multimodal transformer framework that fuses heterogeneous sensor streams, inertial measurement units (IMUs), physiological wearables, skeleton keypoints, and depth imagery, for robust work operation recognition in packaging environments. Our approach employs modality-specific encoders to extract temporal and spatial features from each sensor type, followed by a cross-modal transformer that learns inter-modal dependencies through multi-head self-attention. To further enhance semantic discrimination, we introduce a language-guided alignment module that grounds sensor representations in natural-language descriptions of work operations using a frozen pretrained vision–language text encoder, enabling contrastive semantic supervision at zero inference cost. Experiments on the OpenPack benchmark, reported as the mean ± standard deviation over the five cross-subject splits prescribed by the benchmark protocol, show that PackFormer attains a macro-averaged F1 of 0.891 ± 0.007 across the ten OpenPack work-operation classes. To isolate the source of this gain we re-train every published comparator on the same four modalities, so that architecture and input modality are varied one at a time rather than jointly. This decomposition attributes + 0.026 F1 to the additional modalities and + 0.035 F1 to the PackFormer backbone and its language alignment, relative to the strongest published baseline. An interpretability analysis of the cross-modal attention shows that attention mass allocated to the physiological and depth blocks tracks independent physical proxies for exertion (Spearman ρ = 0.94) and spatial context (ρ = 0.84), converting a previously qualitative claim about modality complementarity into a measurable one. We further quantify sensitivity to prompt wording and assess the feasibility of shop-floor deployment, where INT8 execution reduces the model to 13.9 MB for a cost of 0.007 macro-F1 and a roofline analysis places every platform considered an order of magnitude inside the real-time budget.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.002.title: PackFormer: A multimodal transformer framework with vision–language alignment for industrial work operation recognition in IoT-enabled smart logistics

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.013.abstract: Disassembly is key to circular production, enabling end-of-life products to be recovered through reuse, remanufacturing, or recycling. However, disassembly is characterized by high uncertainty about product condition and process feasibility, which requires dynamic, product-specific planning. While predictive disassembly planning anticipates uncertainties, disassembly systems must additionally be able to adapt their plans in real time when deviations occur. This is addressed by Reactive Disassembly Planning (RDP), which enables the dynamic adaptation of disassembly processes and schedules during disassembly. However, unlocking RDP’s full potential requires complex decision-making based on comprehensive real-time data. To support such data-driven RDP, a modular Digital Twin architecture is presented that integrates all decision-making steps into an automated, real-time planning pipeline. The architecture is instantiated and deployed as a Digital Twin in a learning-factory disassembly system to demonstrate the feasibility and end-to-end operation of the proposed modules and connectors. Its potential is illustrated in a representative scenario, in which the instantiated Digital Twin achieves a 78% reduction in lead time and a 2% increase in profit compared to operating without RDP, and a 529% profit increase compared to a rule-based process-termination strategy. These results serve as illustrative proof of applicability, indicating that data-driven RDP via Digital Twins can support efficient, resilient disassembly operations and thereby strengthen the business case for circular factories and the transition to more sustainable production.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.08.013.title: A modular Digital Twin architecture for the data-driven reactive planning of disassembly systems

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.011.abstract: Conventional fault diagnosis methods primarily focus on improving the recognition accuracy of individual equipment while overlooking differential risks that various faults pose to production line continuity. This accuracy‑oriented paradigm tends to significantly increase unplanned downtime when equipment importance is unevenly distributed, especially in the presence of bottleneck processes. To address this, this paper proposes a production continuity-guided production line‑level health assessment method named unplanned downtime minimization-driven domain-generalized topological transformer (UDMDGTT). From the novel perspective of production continuity, the proposed method quantifies equipment importance and shutdown risks in multi‑process workflows based on Birnbaum importance. A process‑dependent unplanned shutdown risk matrix (USRM) is constructed as a core tool for assessing production continuity, and the downtime cost caused by diagnosis decisions is integrated into the model training process. The USRM is used to construct the production line shutdown risk loss within the UDMDGTT framework, enabling the model to strategically avoid high‑cost misclassifications on critical equipment. To simultaneously pursue accuracy improvement and downtime minimization, a multi‑task loss function with a two‑stage training strategy is designed, and a time‑varying equipment importance mechanism that adapts to process reconfiguration without retraining is introduced to enhance cross‑process generalizability. Experiments on a manufacturing system comprising one lathe and two milling machines demonstrate that UDMDGTT reduces production line downtime while maintaining competitive cross‑domain recognition accuracy. Compared with the ablation model without unplanned downtime minimization, UDMDGTT reduces downtime by 16.88%, 47.08%, and 26.74% on the three machines, respectively, with only minor decreases (1.33%, 0.56%, and 0.72%) in recognition accuracy.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.011.title: A production continuity-guided domain-generalized topological transformer for production line real-time health assessment

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.012.abstract: Human–robot collaboration (HRC) has emerged as a promising assembly paradigm that exploits the complementary capabilities of humans and robots to achieve efficient and flexible task execution. However, existing assembly planning methods still have limited capability in representing dynamic task evolution and often suffer from inefficient policy learning, which restricts their applicability to complex HRC assembly scenarios. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a temporal task graph modeling and multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for HRC assembly sequence planning. First, a dynamic node graph is constructed from assembly-task relationships to represent task precedence, execution states, and human–robot interaction dynamics. Multi-dimensional task evaluation indicators are further incorporated to establish a structured multi-agent learning environment. Based on this environment, a multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm enhanced by temporal graph network (TG-MAPPO) is developed, in which temporal graph representation and multi-agent policy optimization are jointly coupled to improve exploration efficiency and training stability in partially observable dynamic graph environments. To evaluate the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed method, two assembly cases with different task structures, including an electric gripper and an electric vehicle battery (EVB), are used for comparative validation. Furthermore, a physical HRC assembly workstation is established, and a real-world HRC assembly experiment for the electric gripper is conducted. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can generate feasible and efficient HRC assembly sequences. Compared with conventional schemes, the proposed method improves collaborative assembly efficiency, reduces the overall operation time by 44%, and alleviates operator fatigue during task execution.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.012.title: Temporal task graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning for efficient human-robot collaborative assembly planning

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.007.abstract: Additive Manufacturing (AM) is a promising technology for small-volume and customized production. However, the diversity of parts, coupled with batch scheduling and geometric constraints on heterogeneous machines, poses significant challenges for production planning. Unlike most existing studies on AM scheduling that underestimate geometric features, this paper investigates a real-time integrated scheduling and nesting problem with dynamic batch processing and geometric feasibility to minimize the overall makespan across heterogeneous AM machines. We propose GeoPPO, a geometry-aware deep reinforcement learning approach based on Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The proposed approach employs dedicated state encoders and specialized decoders within an actor–critic architecture and potential-based reward shaping strategy to produce geometry-aware decisions for part selection, machine assignment, and batch formulation. Computational experiments are conducted on synthetic and real-world instances with representative AM machine configurations and industrial part geometries. The results show that GeoPPO achieves near-optimal makespan on small-scale instances with an average deviation of 5.3% from the best MILP solutions, while reducing computation time from 1200 s to 1-3 s. With increasing problem scale, GeoPPO outperforms MILP on medium-scale instances, whereas MILP becomes computationally intractable for large-scale problems. Across all instances, GeoPPO reduces makespan by 18.1% relative to the best heuristic, and achieves solution quality comparable to the metaheuristic baseline among GA, ALNS, and GWO, while requiring only about 1% of the computational time. Ablation studies and generalization experiments further demonstrate the efficiency and practical applicability of GeoPPO. This research provides an effective and practical solution paradigm for complex scheduling and nesting challenges in AM.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.007.title: Geometry-aware deep reinforcement learning for real-time integrated scheduling and nesting in additive manufacturing

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.020.abstract: As a key stage in the intelligent manufacturing of commercial aircraft, process planning plays an important role in improving production efficiency and ensuring product quality. Traditional process planning relies heavily on manual review of scattered, frequently updated technical documents, which is not only time-consuming and labor-intensive but also prone to errors due to limited experience. With the development of large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based intelligent process planning methods have achieved significant progress. However, existing RAG-based process planning generation methods typically rely on static one-shot querying and passive filtering. As a result, LLMs lack the ability to autonomously assess knowledge sufficiency, which limits their effectiveness in handling fragmented process knowledge and complex interrelationships. To this end, this paper proposes ProcessLLM-R1, an intelligent method for commercial aircraft assembly process generation based on hypergraph retrieval and reinforcement learning. First, a process knowledge hypergraph is constructed to organize process knowledge, and hypergraph retrieval strategy is designed that can be autonomously invoked by LLM, thereby enhancing the models’ ability to dynamically acquire and organize process knowledge. Second, retrieval is modeled as a multi-round interaction between the agent and knowledge hypergraph, and GRPO is introduced to perform parameter-efficient fine-tuning of the agent, thereby improving its adaptability to process generation tasks. Finally, experimental results on the commercial aircraft machining and assembly process datasets show that ProcessLLM-R1 outperforms the evaluated LLM-based generation and retrieval-augmented baselines across the reported metrics. It is hoped that the research can provide valuable insights and support for the application of LLM-based solutions in the field of aircraft manufacturing.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.020.title: ProcessLLM-R1: A hypergraph retrieval-augmented and reinforcement learning-driven assembly process planning for commercial aircraft
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.020.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.010.abstract: High-precision CNC machining of free-form aerospace components requires bounded compensations informed by inspection, simulation, and process knowledge. Off-the-shelf large language model (LLM) assistants can generate text, but they do not reliably execute risk-constrained multi-step numerical workflows or provide auditable provenance for high-stakes decisions. We present multi-agent knowledge analysis (MAKA), a decision-support architecture that separates intent routing, tools-only quantitative analysis, knowledge graph retrieval, and critic-based verification that enforces physical plausibility, safety bounds, and provenance completeness before recommendations are surfaced for human approval. MAKA is instantiated on a Ti-6Al-4V rotor blade machining testbed by fusing virtual-machining path-tracking error fields, cutting-force and deflection simulations, and scan-based 3D inspection deviation maps from 16 blades. The analysis decomposes deviation into an evidence-linked pathing component, a drift-based wear proxy capturing systematic evolution across parts, and a residual systematic compliance term. In a three-level tool-orchestration benchmark spanning single-step to three-or-more-step stateful sequences, MAKA increased the pass rate for correct tool selection, argument assignment, and dependency-consistent execution by a mean, median, and maximum of 22.9, 8.0, and 64.0 percentage points, respectively, across 15 model-level comparisons over the stronger of the ReAct-style and structured function-calling baselines with identical model and tool access. Digital twin what-if studies show MAKA can coordinate traceable compensation candidates that reduce predicted surface deviation from order 10−2 in to approximately ±10−3 in over most of the blade within the simulation environment, providing a pre-deployment verification signal for risk-aware human decision-making.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.010.title: Physics-grounded multi-agent architecture for traceable, risk-aware human–AI decision support in manufacturing
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.010.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.026.abstract: Manufacturing operation strategy, as a crucial element in part manufacturing, directly impacts processing efficiency and manufacturing quality. Current machine learning-based manufacturing operation decision methods inevitably lose geometric and topological information when converting 3D CAD models into intermediate formats such as point clouds, voxels, or meshes, while also facing the challenge of insufficient training data. To address these issues, this study proposes an innovative hybrid learning approach combining self-supervised pre-training with supervised fine-tuning that learns B-Rep representations from large-scale unlabeled CAD data to achieve manufacturing operation strategy prediction on small-sample datasets. The method consists of two key modules: first, a pre-training model based on an encoder-decoder architecture, where the encoder learns latent representations of CAD model face topological entities, and the decoder reconstructs the signed distance function of model faces; second, a supervised learning phase that utilizes pre-trained facial latent space representations to complete model segmentation tasks based on manufacturing strategies and modeling information using labeled data. Compared to traditional rule-based 3D shape representation sampling methods, directly using B-Rep data representation significantly improves accuracy; compared to existing supervised learning methods based on B-Rep input, the hybrid approach proposed in this study demonstrates superior performance on small-scale training sets.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.026.title: A novel machining operation strategy prediction method based on self-supervised B-rep learning

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.006.abstract: Point-cloud (PC) registration is fundamental to three-dimensional (3D) perception in robotic systems. However, classic registration algorithms falter when aligning a source PC containing limited, incomplete, or ambiguous geometric cues against a reference. This challenge of registering a small, partial PC to a significantly larger global reference is pervasive in real-world deployment yet remains insufficiently addressed by existing learning-based approaches, which typically assume comparable scales and significant overlap. To bridge this gap, we propose the Region-based Small-to-Large Point-cloud Registration framework (R-SLPR), a novel three-stage architecture that fundamentally reformulates the scale-mismatched registration problem into a sequence of region proposal, regional matching, and iterative refinement. Unlike conventional methods that fail to localize specific regions, R-SLPR explicitly identifies candidate regions prior to estimating rigid transformations, ensuring robust alignment even under severe scale mismatch. The framework introduces a Fibonacci Grid Segmentation method coupled with a contrastive learning objective to effectively generate and match local geometric patches. Building on this, a novel Cascade Anchor Selection and Refinement algorithm iteratively aligns the source with the target region to maximize precision. Extensive evaluation on ModelNet40 demonstrates that R-SLPR establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy standard, outperforming prior approaches and significantly reducing translation and rotation Mean Absolute Error (MAE) to 0.009 and 1.104, respectively. For more details and supplementary materials, please visit the companion website of this paper.11https://macs-lab.github.io/R-SLPR/.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.09.006.title: R-SLPR: Region-based Small-to-Large Point-cloud Registration with contrastive learning

10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.10.005.abstract: Existing micro-milling optimization methods often rely on fixed objective weights or direct parameter control, limiting their ability to handle state-dependent trade-offs among surface quality, energy consumption, and machining time. This study proposes a preference-constrained hierarchical actor-critic framework with a learned world model for sequential parameter optimization. Unlike direct-parameter reinforcement learning, the proposed method separates objective-level preference learning from feasible command generation. A high-level Dirichlet policy selects an interpretable preference vector over surface quality, energy, and time, while a constrained inverse control module maps it to spindle speed, feed rate, and depth of cut within prescribed bounds and rate limits. A multimodal temporal convolutional gated recurrent unit (MTC-GRU) world model trained on 900 physical Ti-6Al-4V micro-milling trials serves as the rollout environment for policy learning. Controller performance is evaluated through closed-loop rollouts within the frozen learned environment, while three predetermined variable-parameter trajectories, each physically replayed nine times, are used to assess recursive world-model fidelity under low, medium, and high transition intensities. Within the learned environment, preference-constrained hierarchical actor-critic (PC-HAC) improves surface quality, energy use, and machining time under the stationary objective, and achieves larger gains in the cumulative energy-budget task. At κ = 0.80, PC-HAC reduced the budget-penalized score by 53.9% relative to the greedy controller. The recursive physical replay evaluation yields overall R2 values of 0.810 for surface roughness and 0.975 for energy, with prediction error increasing as transition magnitude increases. These findings support the proposed preference-space control strategy within the investigated micro-milling setting and provide a foundation for future physical closed-loop validation.
10.1016/j.jmsy.2026.10.005.title: Hierarchical reinforcement learning using a world model for multi-objective optimization of micro-milling
